blocks.html: This man said, with Propertius:
I am not moved by tears: I have been caught by that art before. You are always weeping, Cynthia, to lay a snare.

notes.original: Nil moueor lachrymis, iſta ſum capus ab arte. Semper ab inſidiis, Cynthia flere ſoles.
notes.gloss: Nil moveor lacrimis: ista sum captus ab arte; / semper ab insidiis, Cynthia, flere soles — the poet's farewell to Cynthia, the last elegy of book 3, as the orphan note a2 on p106 says.

blocks.html: And in truth, because women seem to be born to weep, and shed tears when it pleases them and seems good to them <sup class="mk" data-key="b" data-page="p107">b</sup>,

notes.gloss: Jason to Medea: a woman is a female thing and born to tears (γυνὴ δὲ θῆλυ κἀπὶ δακρύοις ἔφυ).

blocks.html: They learn to weep becomingly, and they cry at whatever time they wish, and in whatever manner <sup class="mk" data-key="c" data-page="p107">c</sup>.

notes.original: Ouid. au iij de arte amãd.
notes.gloss: Quo non ars penetrat? discunt lacrimare decenter, / quoque volunt plorant tempore quoque modo; the print's Quóq; is quoque with the -que sign. The `⟨alt⟩` iij⟨alt:iiij⟩ is taken as iij: the lines are in book 3, and the Ars has only three books.

blocks.html: One must not at all give credence to their tears, most often feigned, simulated and full of hypocrisy, nor to their words either: for women have (says Plautus) honey on their tongues; but their heart is all covered with gall, sprinkled with vinegar, full of every bitterness <sup class="mk" data-key="d" data-page="p107">d</sup>.

notes.gloss: In melle sunt linguae sitae vostrae atque orationes, / facta atque corda in felle sunt sita atque acerbo aceto. The print's Tuſcul. is a misprint for Trucul.; the `⟨alt⟩` is taken as Plaute (Plautus), Plaure being no name. In Plautus the lines are spoken by the maid Astaphium of men's tongues and hearts; Coras turns them on women.
